newsitem.title: USA: Chain gangs, no coffee in prison Dole visits.
newsitem.headline: Chain gangs, no coffee in prison Dole visits.

text.p: Chain-gang women get no latte in this lock-up.
The Estrella Jail Facility, visited on Tuesday by Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole to dramatise his anti-crime theme, has been established as the epitome of get-tough prisons.
The 1,400 inmates including 200 women live in 66 military surplus tents set up on the desert floor. They work in chain gangs, eat cold bologna and are forbidden to drink coffee.

"This inexpensive alternative to traditional jailing boasts discipline, hard work and the absence of frills as the cornerstone of the jailing system," according to background material distributed by the Dole campaign.

To inmate Robert McManus, 29, a Philadelphia resident serving a five-month sentence for attempted robbery, the main complaint is not the lack of coffee, it's the desert. "It's just, like, the heat. It's constantly hot in here," said McManus, who sported a Marilyn Monroe tattoo and an "MCSO Working Inmate" prison uniform.

The tent city and tough rules were established in 1993 by Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio, a former federal drug agent in Turkey. The tents gave Arpaio a way both to meet a budget squeeze and to carry out a philosophy that prisons should be "humane, but undesireable."
"It's been a great savings to the taxpayer," Arpaio told Dole as he showed off his facility.
Each tent held 10 light green metal bunk beds with thin mattresses. A concrete slab served as the floor. The tent walls were rolled up and inmates lounged on their beds.

"Sheriff Arpaio constantly declares that 'jails shouldn't be hotels' and he backs this statement up with 23-hour lockdowns, a ban on smoking and tobacco use, the elimination of coffee drinking, a prohibition against pornographic magazines and restrictions on television viewing," the campaign description says.
"In addition to these rules, inmates must keep their hair cut short so they cannot hide contraband, are subject to random drug tests and are given sack lunches instead of hot lunches."
And out-of-line prisoners are put to work on chain gangs eight hours a day, six days a week, as "rehabilitation."
"Through the chain gang programme, misbehaving inmates receive a chance to redeem themselves through hard work and community service," the campaign material says.
When Dole stopped by McManus's tent, he asked prisoners if they were coming back. "No way," McManus said. "I've learned my lesson. I don't want to live in these conditions."
But after Dole left, McManus said the problem was a lack of programmes to prepare inmates for outside life and conditions were debilitating. "You walk out of here sometimes hardened."

The politics of the prisoners appeared mixed. "Bill, pack your bags, it's time to go," read a hand-lettered sign on one prisoner's tent. But another was heard shouting as a group of reporters passed, "Four more years."
